choices.text: United nonstop: depart DEN 1:25 p.m., arrive PHX 2:20 p.m., $310.
Southwest nonstop: depart DEN 11:45 a.m., arrive PHX 12:40 p.m., $286.
Delta nonstop: depart DEN 3:20 p.m., arrive PHX 4:15 p.m., $324.
United nonstop: depart DEN 8:50 a.m., arrive PHX 9:45 a.m., $271.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium. The query alone does not rank lower cost and earlier arrival against keeping more of Tuesday free. History is needed both to apply the afternoon-departure preference and to treat United as a nonexclusive tiebreaker rather than a hard carrier rule.
probes.gold_action: Hold A, the 1:25 p.m. United nonstop, first.
probes.label_rationale: A combines an afternoon departure with the soft United preference. C is a genuine alternative because it preserves more of Tuesday, but it costs $14 more and arrives later; within otherwise comparable afternoon options, United can receive positive ranking weight. B and D are cheaper but require departures before the preferred afternoon window. This uses United as a tiebreaker among viable choices, not as a reason to accept a materially worse itinerary.
probes.query: Erin is self-booking a Tuesday Denver-to-Phoenix outbound for a Wednesday 11:00 a.m. client calibration. She has no Tuesday obligation after leaving home, no current-trip carrier instruction, and any listed arrival allows normal hotel check-in and dinner. Each option is a standard-economy nonstop with the same change terms; baggage and seat selection are irrelevant. Which flight should she hold first?

choices.text: United nonstop: depart LAS 2:00 p.m., arrive DEN 4:50 p.m., $273.
Southwest nonstop: depart LAS 11:30 a.m., arrive DEN 2:20 p.m., $250.
Delta nonstop: depart LAS 2:40 p.m., arrive DEN 5:30 p.m., $266.
United nonstop: depart LAS 8:35 a.m., arrive DEN 11:25 a.m., $238.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard. The query alone leaves the small fare difference, 40-minute departure difference, and 40-minute earlier arrival unresolved. History is required to avoid turning either afternoon preference into a latest-flight rule or United preference into exclusive loyalty.
probes.gold_action: Lead the shortlist with A, the 2:00 p.m. United nonstop.
probes.label_rationale: A and C are closely comparable afternoon returns: C saves $7 and leaves 40 minutes later, while A gets Erin home 40 minutes sooner. Neither difference is material, so the soft United preference can favor A without treating United as exclusive. B and D are lower-cost options, but both leave outside the preferred afternoon window; the afternoon consideration is therefore doing real work alongside the carrier preference.
probes.query: Erin is choosing a Sunday Las Vegas-to-Denver return after a personal weekend. She can leave on any listed flight, has no commitment until Monday afternoon, and has given no carrier instruction for this trip. Every option is a standard-economy nonstop with the same relevant fare flexibility and no baggage or seat difference. Which return should lead the shortlist?

choices.text: United via Chicago O'Hare: depart DEN 1:35 p.m., 75-minute connection, arrive DSM 7:50 p.m., $421.
Delta via Minneapolis: depart DEN 11:50 a.m., 70-minute connection, arrive DSM 4:45 p.m., $398.
American via Dallas-Fort Worth: depart DEN 3:20 p.m., 2-hour 10-minute connection, arrive DSM 10:20 p.m., $405.
United via Chicago O'Hare: depart DEN 8:25 a.m., 80-minute connection, arrive DSM 2:40 p.m., $413.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard. The query does not specify how to weight $23, departure time, arrival time, and transfer duration. Selecting A requires jointly applying the afternoon-departure and short-layover preferences, then using United only as a soft positive factor among the still-comparable itineraries.
probes.gold_action: Put A, the afternoon United itinerary via O'Hare, at the top of the working plan.
probes.label_rationale: A is the balanced option: it has an afternoon departure, one short transfer, and a United itinerary. B is a viable cheaper and earlier-arriving alternative, but it gives up the afternoon departure; C leaves later and costs less but creates the notably longer layover and later arrival that Erin normally avoids when a short-transfer option exists; D keeps United and a short transfer but requires a morning departure. A does not use airline preference to justify an ugly route or material itinerary sacrifice.
probes.query: Erin is self-booking a Tuesday Denver-to-Des Moines outbound for a Wednesday 1:00 p.m. client session. She has no Tuesday obligation after leaving home, no equipment case, and no current-trip carrier instruction. All choices are standard economy, have one published-valid connection, and allow hotel check-in Tuesday evening; fare rules, bags, and seats do not differ. Which itinerary belongs at the top of the working plan?
